newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa seeks to control its dogs of war.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seeks to control its dogs of war.

text.p: The South African government on Tuesday presented parliament with draft legislation that would control but not ban outright the activities of mercenary soldiers.

The legislation, approved by the cabinet of President Nelson Mandela in April, was introduced after the government found it had no legal powers to intervene in the operations of Executive Outcomes, a group offering military training to any country willing to pay for it.

Executive Outcomes, staffed largely by former members of the South African defence force, was credited with helping to turn the tide in favour of the Angolan government in its civil war against UNITA. It has also operated in Sierra Leone.

Under the Foreign Military Assistance Bill, anyone wanting to provide military training or other assistance to a foreign country will have to apply to a committee chaired by Kader Asmal, minister of water affairs and forestry.
"There are people who argue that the only way to deal with soldiers of fortune is to ban them outright," Asmal told the parliamentary committee charged with studying the legislation.
"That may well be emotionally satisfying, but as South Africa's shoddy past has demonstrated, the mere fact of a ban does not necessarily amount to effective action.
"We have chosen the route of strict regulation," said Asmal, whose committee also vets South African arms sales.
"It should not be seen as providing a licence for a continuation of doubtful and dangerous activities which were so prevalent in the past," Asmal told the committee.
"It should be seen as a realistic and earnest measure to deal with the situation in accordance with the constitution and in accordance with reasonable norms."
Asmal said past mercenary activity had harmed foreign relations "while enriching generally unsavoury characters".
He said activities covered by the legislation included combat, provision of advice or training, logistics support, recruitment and security services.

"Applications will be refused outright if they may result in the violation or suppression of human rights, endanger peace by destabilising a region, support terrorism, escalate conflict or prejudice South Africa's national or international obligations and interests," Asmal said.
